“I can't, I can't!” Marianne cried. “Leave me if I upset you. Leave me, hate me, forget me! But don't torment me like this. Oh, how easy it is for people with no sorrow of their own to talk about making an effort! Happy, happy Elinor! _You_ cannot imagine what I am suffering.”
“Do you call _me_ happy, Marianne? Ah, if only you knew! And can you really believe I am happy while I see you so wretched?”

“Forgive me, forgive me!” She threw her arms round her sister's neck. “I know you feel for me. I know how loving your heart is. But you are happy—you must be. Edward loves you. What, oh what, could take away happiness like that?”
“A great many things,” Elinor answered gravely.
“No, no, no!” Marianne cried wildly. “He loves you, and only you. You _cannot_ have anything to grieve about.”
“I cannot take pleasure in anything while I see you like this.”
“And you will never see me any other way. Nothing can take away my misery.”

“You must not speak like that, Marianne. Have you no comforts left? No friends? Has your loss left no possibility of consolation? Much as you suffer now, think how much worse it would have been if you had discovered his character later—if he had allowed your engagement to continue for months and months, as he might have done, before choosing to end it. Every extra day of that unhappy trust on your part would have made the eventual blow more dreadful.”
“Engagement!” Marianne exclaimed. “We have never been engaged.”
“Never engaged?”
“No. He is not as dishonourable as you think. He has broken no promise to me.”
“But he did tell you he loved you.”
“Yes—no—not in so many words. It was implied every day, but never explicitly declared. Sometimes I thought he had said it, but he never did.”
“And yet you wrote to him?”
“Yes. After everything that had happened, could that be wrong? But I cannot talk about it.”

Elinor said nothing more. She turned back to the three letters, now far more curious about them than before, and quickly read them all. The first, which Marianne had sent on their arrival in London, ran as follows.
Berkeley Street, January.

“How surprised you will be to receive this, Willoughby! And I think you will feel more than surprise when you learn that I am in London. We could not resist the opportunity to come, even though it meant coming with Mrs. Jennings. I hope you get this in time to visit us tonight, though I shall not count on it. In any case, I shall expect you tomorrow. Goodbye for now.
Her second note, written on the morning after the dance at the Middletons', contained these words:

“I cannot tell you how disappointed I am to have missed you the day before yesterday, or how astonished I am to have received no answer to the note I sent more than a week ago. Every hour of the day I have been expecting to hear from you, and still more to see you. Please come again as soon as you can, and explain why I have been waiting in vain. You had better call earlier next time, because we are usually out by one. Last night we went to Lady Middleton's, where there was a dance. I have been told you were invited. But can that be true? If you could have been invited and stayed away, you must have changed very much since we parted. I will not believe that possible, and hope very soon to hear you assure me yourself that it is not so.
The last note she had sent him read as follows:

“What am I to understand from your behaviour last night, Willoughby? Once again I ask you to explain it. I was ready to greet you with the pleasure that naturally followed our separation, and with the familiarity that our closeness at Barton seemed to justify. How thoroughly I was rejected! I have spent a miserable night trying to excuse behaviour that can hardly be called anything less than insulting. Although I have not yet found any reasonable explanation for it, I am perfectly willing to hear your justification. Perhaps you have been given mistaken information about me, or deliberately deceived about something that has lowered me in your opinion. Tell me what it is. Explain why you acted as you did, and I shall be content if I can satisfy you. It would indeed grieve me to be forced to think badly of you. But if I must—if I am to discover that you are not the man we have believed you, that your affection for us all was insincere, and that you meant only to deceive me by your behaviour—let me know as soon as possible. My feelings are in a dreadful state of uncertainty. I want to believe you innocent, but certainty either way would be a relief compared with what I suffer now. If your feelings have changed, return my notes and the lock of my hair that you have.

For Willoughby's sake, Elinor would have preferred not to believe that letters so full of affection and trust could receive such an answer. But her condemnation of him did not blind her to the impropriety of writing them at all. She silently regretted the recklessness that had risked such uninvited proofs of tenderness, justified by nothing that had gone before and most severely condemned by the outcome. Seeing that Elinor had finished reading, Marianne remarked that the letters contained nothing which anyone in the same position would not have written.
“I felt,” she added, “as solemnly bound to him as if the strictest legal agreement had committed us to each other.”
“I can believe that,” Elinor said. “Unfortunately, he did not feel as you did.”

“He _did_ feel as I did, Elinor. For weeks and weeks he felt it. I know he did. Whatever has changed him now—and only the darkest plotting against me could have done it—I was once as dear to him as my heart could wish. This lock of hair, which he can now give up so easily, he begged me for with the most earnest pleading. If only you had seen his expression, his manner, heard his voice at that moment! Have you forgotten our last evening together at Barton? And the morning we parted! When he told me it might be many weeks before we met again—his distress! Could I ever forget his distress?”
For a moment or two she could say nothing more. When the rush of feeling had passed, she continued in a steadier voice.
“Elinor, I have been treated cruelly, but it was not Willoughby who did it.”
“My dearest Marianne, who else could it be? Who could have urged him to it?”

“The whole world, rather than his own heart. I would sooner believe that everyone I know had joined together to destroy his good opinion of me than that he could be capable of such cruelty. This woman he writes about, whoever she is—or anyone, in fact, except your own dear self, Mama, and Edward—may have been cruel enough to tell lies about me. Apart from you three, is there anyone alive whom I would not sooner suspect of wrongdoing than Willoughby, whose heart I know so well?”

Elinor would not argue. She only said, “Whoever has made themselves your enemy so despicably, my dear sister, deny them their malicious triumph. Let them see how nobly the knowledge of your own innocence and good intentions supports you. The pride that resists such malice is reasonable and deserves respect.”

“No, no!” Marianne cried. “Misery like mine has no pride. I do not care who knows how unhappy I am. The whole world may have the triumph of seeing it. Elinor, people who suffer little may be as proud and independent as they please. They may resist insults, or repay humiliation with humiliation. But I cannot. I must feel, I must be miserable, and anyone who can enjoy knowing it is welcome to do so.”
“But for our mother's sake, and for mine—”
“I would do more than for my own. But to look happy when I am so miserable—oh, who could demand that?”

They both fell silent again. Elinor walked thoughtfully between the fire and the window, and back again, unaware of the warmth from one or the view through the other. Marianne sat at the foot of the bed, her head resting against one of its posts. She picked up Willoughby's letter once more, shuddered over every sentence, and exclaimed,

“It is too much! Oh, Willoughby, could you have written this? Cruel, cruel! Nothing can excuse you. Nothing, Elinor. Whatever he might have heard against me, should he not have withheld his belief? Should he not have told me, and given me a chance to clear myself? ‘The lock of hair you were so kind as to give me’”—she repeated the words from the letter—“that is unforgivable. Willoughby, where was your heart when you wrote those words? Oh, such brutal insolence! Elinor, can anything justify him?”
“No, Marianne. Nothing could possibly justify him.”

“And yet this woman—who knows what tricks she has used? How long she may have planned it, how carefully she may have plotted! Who is she? Who can she be? Which of his female acquaintances did I ever hear him describe as young and attractive? Oh, nobody, nobody! He spoke to me only about myself.”
Another silence followed. Marianne was deeply agitated, and at last broke it with these words.
“Elinor, I must go home. I must go back and comfort Mama. Could we not leave tomorrow?”
“Leave tomorrow, Marianne?”
“Yes. Why should I stay here? I came only because of Willoughby. And now who cares about me? Who feels for me?”
“We could not possibly leave tomorrow. We owe Mrs. Jennings much more than mere politeness; and even the most ordinary politeness would prevent us from making such a hurried departure.”

“Well, perhaps in another day or two, then. But I cannot stay long. I cannot remain here to endure all these people's questions and remarks. The Middletons and Palmers—how am I to bear their pity? To be pitied by a woman like Lady Middleton! Oh, what would _he_ say to that?”

Elinor urged her to lie down again, and for a moment she did. But no position brought relief. Restless with pain in both mind and body, she shifted continually from one posture to another. As she grew increasingly distraught, Elinor could barely keep her on the bed and for some time feared she would have to call for help. At last Marianne was persuaded to take some lavender drops, which helped her. From then until Mrs. Jennings returned, she lay quietly on the bed without moving.

chapters.title: Chapter 30
paragraphs: As soon as Mrs. Jennings returned, she came to their room. She asked to be let in, but without waiting for an answer opened the door and entered, looking genuinely concerned.
“How are you feeling, my dear?” she asked Marianne with great sympathy. Marianne turned her face away, making no attempt to answer her.

“How is she, Miss Dashwood? Poor thing, she looks very ill. And no wonder! Yes, it is all too true. He is getting married very soon—the worthless fellow! I have no patience with him. Mrs. Taylor told me half an hour ago, and she heard it from a close friend of Miss Grey herself. Otherwise I should never have believed it. As it was, I nearly dropped on the spot. Well, I said, if this is true, all I can say is that he has treated a young lady I know abominably, and I hope with all my heart his wife makes his life a misery. And you may depend on it, my dear, that is what I shall always say. I cannot stand men behaving like this. If ever I meet him again, I shall give him a scolding such as he hasn't had in many a day. But there is one comfort, my dear Miss Marianne: he is not the only young man in the world worth having. With your pretty face, you will never be short of admirers. Well, poor creature, I won't disturb her any longer. She had better have her cry out and be done with it. Fortunately, the Parrys and Sandersons are coming tonight, you know, and that will cheer her up.”
She went away, tiptoeing out of the room as though she imagined that noise might add to her young friend's distress.

To Elinor's surprise, Marianne decided to join them for dinner. Elinor even advised against it. But no: she would go down, she could bear it perfectly well, and there would be less fuss about her. Elinor was pleased to see her guided, even briefly, by such a consideration. Though she hardly believed Marianne could remain through the meal, she said no more. While her sister still lay on the bed, she straightened her dress as well as she could, then stood ready to help her into the dining room when they were called.

Once there, though looking utterly miserable, Marianne ate more and remained calmer than Elinor had expected. If she had tried to speak, or noticed half Mrs. Jennings's well-meant but ill-judged attentions, she could not have kept that calm. But not a word passed her lips, and her absorption in her own thoughts kept her unaware of everything happening around her.

Elinor fully appreciated Mrs. Jennings's kindness, though its expressions often caused distress and sometimes came close to being ridiculous. She offered the thanks and returned the courtesies which Marianne could neither offer nor return for herself. Their good friend saw that Marianne was unhappy, and felt she deserved everything that might make her less so. She therefore treated her with all the indulgent affection a parent shows a favourite child on the last day of the holidays. Marianne must have the best seat by the fire; every delicacy in the house must tempt her to eat; all the day's news must be related for her entertainment. Had her sister's sorrowful face not checked every impulse to laugh, Elinor might have been amused by Mrs. Jennings's attempts to cure disappointed love with sweets, olives, and a good fire. But once the constant repetition of these attentions forced them upon Marianne's notice, she could stay no longer. With a hurried cry of misery, and a gesture telling her sister not to follow, she rose and rushed from the room.

“Poor soul!” Mrs. Jennings cried once she had gone. “How it hurts me to see her! And just look, she has left without finishing her wine! Or her dried cherries! Lord, nothing seems to help her at all. If I knew anything she wanted, I would send all over London to find it. Well, I cannot understand how a man can treat such a pretty girl so badly. But when there is plenty of money on one side and next to none on the other, bless you, they care nothing about such things!”
“So the lady—Miss Grey, I think you called her—is very wealthy?”

“Fifty thousand pounds, my dear. Have you ever seen her? They say she is smart and fashionable, though not beautiful. I remember her aunt very well, Biddy Henshawe. She married a very rich man. But the whole family has money. Fifty thousand pounds! And from everything one hears, it won't arrive a moment too soon, for they say he is quite ruined. No wonder, racing about with his curricle and his hunting horses! Well, there is no use talking. But when a young man, whoever he may be, courts a pretty girl and promises to marry her, he has no right to go back on his word simply because he becomes poor and a richer girl will take him. Why doesn't he sell his horses, rent out his house, dismiss his servants, and reform his whole way of living at once? I am sure Miss Marianne would have waited until his affairs improved. But that will not do nowadays. The young men of this age cannot give up a single pleasure.”
“Do you know what Miss Grey is like as a person? Do people say she is pleasant?”

“I have never heard anything against her. Indeed, I have hardly heard her mentioned, except that Mrs. Taylor said this morning that Miss Walker once hinted to her that she believed Mr. and Mrs. Ellison would be glad to see Miss Grey married, because she and Mrs. Ellison could never get along.”
“And who are Mr. and Mrs. Ellison?”

“Her guardians, my dear. But she is of age now and can choose for herself. And a fine choice she has made!” After a moment's pause, she continued, “Well, I suppose your poor sister has gone to her room to grieve alone. Is there nothing we can get to comfort her? Poor dear, it seems positively cruel to leave her by herself. We shall have a few friends here later, and that will entertain her a little. What shall we play? I know she hates whist, but isn't there some round game she enjoys?”
“My dear ma'am, you need not go to all this trouble. I doubt Marianne will come out of her room again tonight. If I can, I shall persuade her to go to bed early. I am sure she needs rest.”

“Yes, I believe that will be best. Let her choose her own supper and go to bed. Lord, no wonder she has looked so ill and so low these last couple of weeks! I suppose this has been hanging over her all that time. And today's letter finished it! Poor soul! If I had had the least idea, I would not have teased her about it for all the money I possess. But how could I have guessed? I was certain it was only an ordinary love letter, and you know young people like being laughed at about those. Lord, how distressed Sir John and my daughters will be when they hear! If I had been thinking properly, I could have called in Conduit Street on my way home and told them. But I shall see them tomorrow.”

“I am sure you need hardly warn Mrs. Palmer and Sir John against mentioning Mr. Willoughby, or making the slightest reference to what has happened, in front of my sister. Their own kindness must show them how cruel it would be to appear to know anything about it in her presence. And the less that is said to me on the subject, the more my own feelings will be spared, as I know you will readily understand, dear ma'am.”

“Oh, Lord, yes, of course I do! It must be dreadful for you to hear people discussing it. And as for your sister, I would not say a word to her about it for the world. You saw that I never did throughout dinner. Neither would Sir John or my daughters, for they are all very thoughtful and considerate, particularly if I give them a hint, which I certainly shall. For myself, I think the less said about such things, the better: they blow over and are forgotten all the sooner. And what good does talking ever do?”

“In this case it can only do harm, perhaps more than in many similar cases. There are circumstances which, for the sake of everyone involved, make it especially unsuitable for public discussion. I must do Mr. Willoughby _this_ justice: he has broken no definite engagement with my sister.”
“Good gracious, my dear, don't try to defend him! No definite engagement, indeed! After taking her all over Allenham House and choosing the very rooms they were to live in together!”

For Marianne's sake, Elinor could not pursue the subject. She hoped she was not obliged to do so for Willoughby's, since insisting on the precise truth could benefit him very little and cost Marianne a great deal. They were both silent for a short time. Then Mrs. Jennings burst out again with all her natural good humour.

“Well, my dear, the saying about an ill wind is true enough, for all this will be better for Colonel Brandon. He will have her in the end, yes, he will. Mark my words, they will be married by midsummer. Lord, how he will chuckle at the news! I hope he comes tonight. He would be a far better match for your sister. Two thousand a year, without debts or deductions—except that little child of his born out of wedlock; yes, I had forgotten her. But an apprenticeship could be found for her at very little expense, and then what would it matter? Delaford is a lovely place, I can tell you. Exactly what I call a lovely, old-fashioned place, full of comforts and conveniences. Great garden walls enclose it, covered with the finest fruit trees in the country. And there is such a mulberry tree in one corner! Lord, how Charlotte and I ate the only time we visited! Then there is a dovecote, some delightful fish ponds, and a very pretty canal—everything one could wish for, in short. Besides, it is close to the church and only a quarter of a mile from the toll road. It is never dull: you have only to sit in an old yew-tree arbour behind the house, and you can watch all the passing carriages. Oh, it is a lovely place! A butcher close by in the village, and the parsonage within a stone's throw. To my mind, it is a thousand times prettier than Barton Park, where they have to send three miles for meat and have no neighbour nearer than your mother. Well, I shall encourage the Colonel as soon as I can. One shoulder of mutton drives another down, as they say. If only we _can_ put Willoughby out of her mind!”

“Yes, ma'am, if we can do _that_,” Elinor said, “we shall do very well, with or without Colonel Brandon.” She rose and went to join Marianne. As she expected, she found her in their room, leaning in silent misery over the remains of a small fire, which had been her only light until Elinor entered.
“You had better leave me alone,” was the only acknowledgement Marianne gave of her sister's arrival.

“I will leave you if you go to bed,” Elinor answered. At first Marianne refused, with the momentary stubbornness of someone made impatient by suffering. But her sister's earnest, gentle persuasion soon softened her resistance. Before leaving her, Elinor saw her lay her aching head on the pillow and hoped that she was at last ready for some quiet sleep.
Elinor then went to the drawing room. Mrs. Jennings soon joined her, carrying a wineglass filled with something in her hand.

“My dear,” she said as she entered, “I have just remembered that there is some of the finest old Constantia wine imaginable in the house, so I have brought your sister a glass. My poor husband was so fond of it! Whenever his old gout troubled his stomach, he said it did him more good than anything else in the world. Do take it up to her.”

“How kind you are, dear ma'am,” Elinor replied, smiling at the difference between the ailments for which it was recommended. “But I have just left Marianne in bed, and I hope she is nearly asleep. Nothing could help her as much as rest, I think. So, if you will allow me, I shall drink the wine myself.”

Mrs. Jennings regretted being five minutes too late, but accepted the compromise. As Elinor drank most of the glass, she reflected that, although its effect on gout of the stomach mattered little to her at present, its power to heal a disappointed heart might as reasonably be tested on herself as on her sister.

Colonel Brandon arrived while they were having tea. From the way he looked round the room for Marianne, Elinor immediately suspected that he neither expected nor wished to find her there, and that he already knew the reason for her absence. Mrs. Jennings had no such thought. Soon after he entered, she crossed to the tea table, where Elinor was serving, and whispered, “You see, the Colonel looks as solemn as ever. He knows nothing about it. Do tell him, my dear.”
Shortly afterwards he drew a chair beside Elinor's and asked after her sister, with an expression that left her in no doubt that he already knew.
“Marianne is unwell,” she said. “She has felt ill all day, and we have persuaded her to go to bed.”
“Then perhaps,” he answered hesitantly, “what I heard this morning may be—there may be more truth in it than I could at first believe possible.”
“What have you heard?”
“That a gentleman whom I had reason to think—in short, that a man whom I _knew_ to be engaged—but how can I tell you? If you already know, as surely you must, perhaps you can spare me.”

“You mean Mr. Willoughby's marriage to Miss Grey,” Elinor answered with forced calm. “Yes, we _do_ know everything. This seems to have been a day of revelations for everyone, since we first learnt of it this very morning. Mr. Willoughby is impossible to understand! Where did you hear the news?”

“In a stationer's shop in Pall Mall, where I had business. Two ladies were waiting for their carriage. One was telling the other about the proposed marriage in a voice so plainly unconcerned with secrecy that I could not avoid hearing everything. The repeated name, Willoughby—John Willoughby—first attracted my attention. Then came a definite statement that everything concerning his marriage to Miss Grey was finally settled. It was no longer a secret; it would take place within a few weeks. There followed many details of preparations and other arrangements. I remember one point especially, because it made his identity still more certain: immediately after the ceremony they were to go to Combe Magna, his estate in Somersetshire. My astonishment—but I cannot describe what I felt. I stayed in the shop until the ladies had gone, then asked who the talkative one was. Her name was Mrs. Ellison, which I have since been told is the name of Miss Grey's guardian.”
“It is. But have you also heard that Miss Grey has fifty thousand pounds? If anything can explain it, perhaps that can.”
“Perhaps. But Willoughby is capable—at least, I think—” He paused, then continued in a voice that seemed to distrust itself. “And your sister—how did she—”

“She has suffered terribly. I can only hope her suffering will be correspondingly brief. It has been, and still is, a most cruel blow. Until yesterday, I believe she never doubted his love. Even now, perhaps—but _I_ am almost persuaded that he never really loved her. He has been very dishonest, and in some respects there seems a hardness in his heart.”
“Ah!” Colonel Brandon said. “There certainly is. But your sister does not—I think that was what you said—she does not quite see it as you do?”
“You know her nature. You can imagine how eagerly she would still defend him if she could.”

He gave no answer. Soon the tea things were cleared and the card parties arranged, so the subject had to be dropped. Mrs. Jennings had watched their conversation with pleasure. She expected Elinor's news to produce an immediate burst of gaiety in Colonel Brandon, of the kind natural to a young man in the first bloom of hope and happiness. To her astonishment, he remained more serious and thoughtful than usual for the entire evening.

chapters.title: Chapter 31
paragraphs: After a night in which she slept more than she had expected, Marianne woke the next morning to the same awareness of misery with which she had closed her eyes.

Elinor encouraged her as much as she could to speak about her feelings. Before breakfast was ready, they had discussed the whole matter over and over, with the same steady convictions and loving advice from Elinor, and the same passionate emotions and changing opinions from Marianne. Sometimes Marianne could believe Willoughby as unfortunate and innocent as herself; at other times, the impossibility of defending him robbed her of every comfort. One moment she cared nothing for the notice of the whole world; the next she wanted to hide from it for ever; a moment later she could face it with spirit. In one respect, however, her conduct was consistent: whenever possible, she avoided Mrs. Jennings, and when forced to endure her presence she remained determinedly silent. She refused to believe that Mrs. Jennings could feel any real compassion for her sorrow.
“No, no, it is impossible,” she cried. “She cannot feel. Her kindness is not sympathy; her good nature is not tenderness. Gossip is all she wants, and she only likes me now because I provide it.”

Elinor had needed no further proof of the unfair judgements her sister so often made of others. They sprang from the sensitive fastidiousness of her own mind, and the excessive importance she gave to delicate feeling and polished manners. Like half the world—if indeed more than half is intelligent and good—Marianne possessed excellent abilities and an excellent nature, yet was neither reasonable nor fair-minded. She expected everyone else to share her opinions and feelings, and judged their motives by the immediate effect their actions had on herself. Thus, while the sisters were in their room after breakfast, an incident occurred which lowered Mrs. Jennings's heart still further in Marianne's opinion. Through Marianne's own weakness, it happened to cause her fresh pain, although Mrs. Jennings acted from the kindest possible impulse.
She entered their room holding out a letter, her face bright with the smile of someone certain she was bringing comfort, and said,
“Now, my dear, I have brought you something that is sure to make you feel better.”

Marianne had heard enough. In an instant she imagined a letter from Willoughby, full of tenderness and repentance, explaining everything that had happened in a satisfying, convincing way. Immediately after it, Willoughby himself would rush eagerly into the room and fall at her feet, his eloquent eyes confirming every assurance in the letter. What one moment created, the next destroyed. Before her lay her mother's handwriting, never unwelcome until now. The disappointment following that ecstasy, which had been more than hope, was so sharp that she felt she had never truly suffered before.

Even at her most eloquent, Marianne could have found no words adequate to Mrs. Jennings's cruelty. Now she could reproach her only with the passionate torrent of tears streaming from her eyes. The reproach entirely missed its target: after many expressions of sympathy, Mrs. Jennings withdrew, still urging her to look to the comforting letter. But when Marianne was calm enough to read it, the letter brought little comfort. Willoughby filled every page. Her mother remained certain of their engagement, and as confident as ever of his faithfulness. Elinor's appeal had done no more than prompt her to beg Marianne to be more open with them both. She did so with such tenderness towards Marianne, such affection for Willoughby, and such certainty of their future happiness together that Marianne wept in anguish throughout her reading.

Her impatience to return home came back in full force. Her mother was dearer than ever to her—dearer for the very excess of that mistaken trust in Willoughby—and she urgently, almost frantically, insisted on leaving. Elinor could not decide whether London or Barton would be better for Marianne. She offered no advice beyond asking her to wait patiently until they knew their mother's wishes. At last she persuaded her sister to agree to that delay.

Mrs. Jennings went out earlier than usual, unable to rest until the Middletons and Palmers could grieve as much as she did. She firmly refused Elinor's offer to accompany her and left alone for the rest of the morning. With a very heavy heart, Elinor sat down to tell her mother what had happened and ask what they should do next. She knew the pain her letter must cause, and Marianne's letter from home had shown how completely she had failed to prepare the ground. Marianne came into the drawing room when Mrs. Jennings left, and stayed beside the table where Elinor wrote. She watched the progress of her pen, grieving for her sister over the difficulty of the task, and grieving still more tenderly over its effect upon their mother.
They had been like this for about fifteen minutes when a knock at the door startled Marianne, whose nerves could not bear any sudden noise.
“Who can that be?” Elinor exclaimed. “And so early! I thought we _were_ safe from visitors.”
Marianne went over to the window.
“It is Colonel Brandon!” she said irritably. “We are never safe from _him_.”
“He won't come in when he hears Mrs. Jennings is out.”
“I won't depend on _that_,” Marianne said, retreating to her room. “A man with nothing to occupy his own time has no scruples about imposing on other people's.”

Events proved her prediction right, although it rested on an unfair and mistaken judgement: Colonel Brandon _did_ come in. Elinor was certain that concern for Marianne had brought him. She saw it in his troubled, melancholy face and in his anxious, though brief, inquiry after her sister. She could not forgive Marianne for thinking so little of him.

“I met Mrs. Jennings in Bond Street,” he said after greeting her, “and she encouraged me to come on. I needed little persuasion, because I thought I might find you alone, which I very much wished to do. My purpose—my wish—my only wish in wanting that—I hope, I believe it is—is to help bring comfort. No, I must not say comfort, not immediate comfort, but certainty, lasting certainty to your sister's mind. My affection for her, for you, for your mother—will you let me prove it by telling you some circumstances which only _very_ sincere affection, only an earnest desire to be useful—I think I am justified. Yet when I have spent so many hours persuading myself that I am right, is there not some reason to fear I may be wrong?” He stopped.

“I understand,” Elinor said. “You have something to tell me about Mr. Willoughby that will reveal more of his character. Telling it will be the greatest kindness anyone could do Marianne. You will earn _my_ gratitude at once with any information that helps towards that end, and in time you must earn _hers_. Please, please let me hear it.”

“You shall. To put it briefly, when I left Barton last October—but that will explain nothing. I must begin further back. You will find me a very clumsy storyteller, Miss Dashwood. I scarcely know where to start. I think I must give you a short account of myself, and it _shall_ be short.” He sighed deeply. “On such a subject I have little temptation to dwell at length.”
He paused to gather his thoughts, then sighed again and continued.

“You have probably forgotten a conversation—it could hardly have made much impression on you—that we had one evening at Barton Park. It was the evening of a dance. I mentioned a lady I had once known, who seemed to me in some ways to resemble your sister Marianne.”
“I assure you,” Elinor answered, “I have _not_ forgotten it.” He seemed pleased that she remembered, and went on.

“Unless the uncertainty and fond partiality of memory mislead me, they resemble each other very strongly, in character as well as appearance. There is the same warmth of heart, the same lively imagination and eagerness of spirit. The lady was a close relation of mine, orphaned in infancy and placed under my father's guardianship. We were nearly the same age, and from our earliest childhood we were playmates and friends. I cannot remember a time when I did not love Eliza. As we grew older, my love became something you might think me incapable of ever having felt, judging by my present lonely and joyless seriousness. Her love for me was, I believe, as passionate as your sister's for Mr. Willoughby. And, though for a different reason, it was equally unfortunate. At seventeen, she was lost to me for ever. She married—against her wishes—my brother. She had a large fortune; our family estate was heavily burdened with debt. I am afraid that is all that can be said in defence of a man who was both her uncle and her guardian. My brother did not deserve her. He did not even love her. I had hoped that her love for me would carry her through any difficulty, and for a time it did. But at last the misery of her position, for she was treated with great unkindness, broke down her determination. Although she had promised me that nothing—but how badly I tell this! I have never explained how it came about. We were only a few hours away from running off together to Scotland. My cousin's maid betrayed us, through either treachery or foolishness. I was sent away to a relation's house at a great distance. Eliza was denied all freedom, company, and amusement until my father had gained his purpose. I had relied too much on her strength, and it was a severe blow. But if her marriage had been happy, young as I was, a few months must have reconciled me to it; at least, I should not still have cause to mourn it now. That was not what happened. My brother cared nothing for her. His pleasures were not what they should have been, and from the beginning he treated her cruelly. The effect on someone as young, lively, and inexperienced as Mrs. Brandon was only too natural. At first she submitted to all the misery of her position. It would have been better if she had not lived to overcome the sorrow that remembering me caused her. But can we wonder that she fell, with such a husband encouraging unfaithfulness, and no friend to advise or restrain her? My father died only a few months after the wedding, and I was with my regiment in the East Indies. Had I stayed in England, perhaps—but I meant to make us both happier by removing myself from her for years, and had arranged my transfer for that reason. The shock of her marriage,” he continued, his voice greatly agitated, “was a small thing—nothing—compared with what I felt when, about two years later, I heard of her divorce. It was _that_ which cast this gloom—even now, the memory of what I suffered—”

He could say no more. Rising quickly, he walked about the room for several minutes. Elinor was moved by his story, and still more by his suffering, and could not speak. He noticed her concern, came towards her, took her hand, pressed it, and kissed it with grateful respect. A few more minutes of silent effort allowed him to continue calmly.

“Nearly three years passed after that unhappy time before I returned to England. Naturally, my first concern when I _did_ arrive was to find her. But the search was as unsuccessful as it was distressing. I could trace her no further than the first man who had seduced her. There was every reason to fear that she had left him only to sink further into a life of wrongdoing. The allowance legally assigned to her was neither proportionate to her fortune nor sufficient to keep her comfortably. My brother told me that some months earlier she had transferred the right to receive it to someone else. He supposed—and could suppose it quite calmly—that extravagance and the hardship it caused had forced her to sell it for immediate relief. At last, after six months in England, I _did_ find her. Affection for a former servant who had since fallen on hard times took me to visit him in a debtors' holding house. There, in the same building and under the same confinement, was my unfortunate sister-in-law. So changed, so faded, worn down by every kind of acute suffering! I could hardly believe that the sickly, sorrowful figure before me was all that remained of the lovely, healthy, blooming girl I had once adored. What I felt on seeing her—but I have no right to hurt you by trying to describe it. I have already caused you too much pain. That she appeared to be in the final stage of consumption was—yes, in those circumstances—my greatest comfort. Life could offer her nothing except time to prepare better for death, and she was given that time. I arranged comfortable lodgings and proper care for her. I visited her every day of the short life that remained, and I was with her when she died.”
Again he paused to recover himself. Elinor expressed her feelings in a few words of tender concern for the fate of his unfortunate friend.

“I hope your sister would not be offended,” he said, “by the resemblance I have imagined between her and my poor, disgraced relation. Their fates and circumstances cannot be the same. If the natural sweetness of the one had been protected by a stronger mind or a happier marriage, she might have become everything you will live to see the other become. But where is all this leading? I seem to have distressed you for nothing. Ah, Miss Dashwood, a subject like this, untouched for fourteen years—it is dangerous to approach it at all! I _will_ be more composed, more concise. She entrusted her only child to me, a little girl of about three, born from her first affair. She loved the child and had always kept her with her. It was a precious trust to me. Gladly would I have fulfilled it in the fullest sense, overseeing her education myself, if our circumstances had allowed. But I had neither family nor home, and so my little Eliza was sent to school. I visited her whenever I could. After my brother's death, about five years ago, when I inherited the family property, she visited me at Delaford. I described her as a distant relation, though I know very well that people have generally suspected a much closer connection. Three years ago, when she had just turned fourteen, I took her from school and placed her with a very respectable woman in Dorsetshire who looked after four or five other girls of about the same age. For two years I had every reason to be satisfied with the arrangement. But last February, almost a year ago, she suddenly disappeared. At her earnest request, I had allowed her—unwisely, as it turned out—to go to Bath with a young friend whose father was there for his health. I knew him as a very good sort of man, and thought well of his daughter: better than she deserved. With stubborn, ill-judged secrecy she would tell me nothing and give me no clue, though she certainly knew everything. Her father was well-meaning but not observant, and I believe he truly had no information to give. He had mostly been confined to the house while the girls wandered about the town, making whatever acquaintances they pleased. He tried to convince me, as completely as he had convinced himself, that his daughter had nothing to do with the affair. In short, I could learn only that Eliza was gone. Everything else remained a matter of conjecture for eight long months. You may imagine what I thought, what I feared, and what I suffered.”
“Good heavens!” Elinor cried. “Could it be—could Willoughby have—”

“The first news of her,” he continued, “came in a letter she wrote herself, last October. It was forwarded from Delaford, and reached me on the very morning of our planned outing to Whitwell. That was why I left Barton so suddenly. I am sure my departure seemed strange to everyone, and I believe it offended some. When Mr. Willoughby's looks reproached me for the discourtesy of breaking up the party, I suppose he little imagined that I was being called away to help someone he had made destitute and miserable. But if he _had_ known, what difference would it have made? Would he have been less cheerful, or taken less pleasure in your sister's smiles? No. He had already done what no man capable of feeling for another could do. He had seduced a young, innocent girl, then abandoned her in the deepest distress, without a respectable home, without help or friends, and without even knowing his address. He left her with a promise to return. He neither returned, nor wrote, nor sent assistance.”
“This is worse than anything!” Elinor exclaimed.

“Now you know his character: extravagant, dissolute, and worse than either. Knowing all this, as I have for many weeks, imagine what I felt when I saw your sister as fond of him as ever and was assured she would marry him. Imagine what I felt for all of you. When I came last week and found you alone, I was determined to discover the truth, though uncertain what to do once I _had_ discovered it. My behaviour must have seemed strange then, but you will understand it now. To let you all remain so deceived, to see your sister—but what could I do? I had no hope that intervention would succeed. Sometimes I thought her influence might yet reform him. But now, after such dishonourable treatment, who can say what his intentions towards her were? Whatever they may have been, she can now, and surely one day _will_, feel grateful for her own position when she compares it with my poor Eliza's. Let her consider that poor girl's miserable, hopeless circumstances; picture her still loving him as strongly as Marianne does herself, with a mind tormented by self-reproach that must follow her throughout her life. Surely that comparison must help her. She will feel her own suffering is nothing. It comes from no wrongdoing, and can bring no disgrace. On the contrary, it must make every friend more deeply her friend. Sympathy for her unhappiness and respect for her courage in bearing it must strengthen every attachment. Still, use your own judgement in deciding what to tell her of this. You know best what effect it will have. But if I had not sincerely and wholeheartedly believed that it might help her and lessen her regret, I would never have troubled you with this history of my family's suffering—with an account which may seem intended to raise me in your opinion at someone else's expense.”
Elinor thanked him with deep and earnest gratitude. She also assured him that she expected Marianne to benefit greatly from hearing what he had told her.

“Her attempts to defend him have distressed me more than anything else,” she said. “They disturb her mind more than complete certainty of his worthlessness could do. She will suffer greatly at first, but I am sure she will soon find more peace.” After a brief silence, she continued, “Have you ever seen Mr. Willoughby since you left him at Barton?”
“Yes,” he answered gravely. “I have seen him once. One meeting could not be avoided.”
Startled by his manner, Elinor looked at him anxiously and asked,
“What? Did you meet him to—”

“I could meet him in no other way. Eliza had told me her lover's name, though very reluctantly. When he returned to London, within a fortnight of my own arrival, we met by arrangement: he to defend his conduct, I to punish it. Neither of us was wounded, so the meeting never became public knowledge.”
Elinor sighed at the supposed necessity for such a meeting, but did not presume to criticise it to a man who was also a soldier.
“Such,” Colonel Brandon said after a pause, “has been the unhappy likeness between the mother's fate and the daughter's. And how poorly I have fulfilled the trust placed in me!”
“Is she in London still?”
“No. I found her close to giving birth. As soon as she had recovered afterwards, I took her and her baby into the country, and she remains there.”

Soon afterwards he remembered that he was probably keeping Elinor from her sister, and brought his visit to an end. She thanked him again with the same gratitude. He left her filled with compassion for him and with deep respect.

chapters.title: Chapter 32
paragraphs: Elinor soon repeated the details of this conversation to her sister, but its effect was not quite what she had hoped. Marianne did not seem to doubt any part of the story. She listened throughout with steady, unresisting attention, made no objection or comment, and attempted no defence of Willoughby. Her tears appeared to acknowledge that no defence was possible. This assured Elinor that her sister _had_ become convinced of his guilt. She was also pleased to see that Marianne no longer avoided Colonel Brandon when he called, and spoke to him—even of her own accord—with a kind of compassionate respect. Her feelings were less violently disturbed than before. Yet Elinor did not find her any less miserable. Her mind had settled, but into dark dejection. The loss of Willoughby's good character weighed on her even more heavily than the loss of his love. His seduction and abandonment of Miss Williams, the poor girl's suffering, and the uncertainty about what he might _once_ have intended towards herself preyed so deeply on her spirits that she could not speak of her feelings even to Elinor. Brooding silently over her sorrow, she caused her sister more pain than the fullest and most frequent confession could have done.

To describe Mrs. Dashwood's feelings and words when she received and answered Elinor's letter would merely repeat what her daughters had already felt and said. Her disappointment was scarcely less painful than Marianne's, and her indignation even greater than Elinor's. Long letters followed one another rapidly, expressing everything she suffered and thought, her anxious concern for Marianne, and her plea that the girl should bear this misfortune with courage. Marianne's suffering must indeed be terrible when her mother could speak of fortitude! Those regrets must have a humiliating and mortifying cause if even _she_ could wish her daughter not to indulge them!

Putting aside her own comfort, Mrs. Dashwood decided that Marianne would be better anywhere just then than at Barton. Everything she saw there would revive the past in the strongest and most painful way, constantly bringing Willoughby before her as she had always known him there. She therefore strongly urged her daughters not to shorten their visit to Mrs. Jennings. Though its duration had never been precisely fixed, everyone had expected it to last at least five or six weeks. London would inevitably provide a variety of occupations, sights, and company which Barton could not offer. She hoped these might still draw Marianne, now and then, into an interest outside herself, or even into some enjoyment, however firmly she might reject both ideas at present.

Her mother thought Marianne at least as safe from the risk of meeting Willoughby in London as in the country, since anyone claiming to be her friend must now give up his acquaintance. Nobody could deliberately bring them together; nobody's carelessness could expose her to an unexpected meeting. And chance had less opportunity in London's crowds than even in Barton's seclusion. There she might be forced to see him when he paid the wedding visit to Allenham which Mrs. Dashwood had first considered probable, and had gradually persuaded herself was certain.

She had another reason for wanting her daughters to stay where they were. A letter from her stepson said that he and his wife would be in London before the middle of February, and she thought it right that the girls should sometimes see their brother.

Marianne had promised to follow her mother's judgement, and therefore accepted it without protest. It was entirely contrary to both her wishes and her expectations. She believed it completely mistaken, based on false assumptions. By requiring her to remain in London, it denied her the only possible relief for her unhappiness—her mother's sympathy in person—and condemned her to company and surroundings that must prevent her from ever finding a moment's peace.

Still, it was a great comfort to think that what hurt her would benefit her sister. Elinor, for her part, suspected she would not be able to avoid Edward altogether. She consoled herself with the thought that, although their longer stay would therefore work against her own happiness, it would be better for Marianne than an immediate return to Devonshire.

Her care in protecting Marianne from hearing Willoughby's name had not been wasted. Without knowing it, Marianne enjoyed the full benefit: neither Mrs. Jennings, Sir John, nor even Mrs. Palmer ever mentioned him in her presence. Elinor wished the same restraint could have been extended to herself. That was impossible, however, and day after day she had to listen to their collective indignation.

Sir John could never have believed it possible. “A man he had always had such good reason to think well of! Such a good-natured fellow! He did not believe there was a more daring rider in England. The whole business was incomprehensible. He wished him to the devil with all his heart. Wherever they met, he would not say another word to him for anything in the world! Not even if they stood beside the Barton coverts with two hours of waiting ahead of them. What a scoundrel! What a deceitful dog! Only the last time they met he had offered him one of Folly's puppies—and this was how it ended!”

Mrs. Palmer was equally angry in her own way. “She was determined to give up his acquaintance at once, and very thankful that she had never known him at all. She heartily wished Combe Magna were not so close to Cleveland. But it did not matter, because it was much too far away for visits. She hated him so much that she would never mention his name again, and she would tell everyone she met what a worthless man he was.”

Mrs. Palmer showed the rest of her sympathy by collecting every available detail about the approaching wedding and passing it on to Elinor. Before long she could name the coachmaker building the new carriage, the artist painting Mr. Willoughby's portrait, and the shop where Miss Grey's wedding clothes could be seen.

Lady Middleton's calm, polite indifference was a welcome relief to Elinor, whose spirits were often overwhelmed by the others' noisy kindness. It was a great comfort to know that at least _one_ person in their circle felt no interest in the affair; that _one_ person would meet her without curiosity about the details, or anxious inquiries after her sister's health.

The circumstances of a moment can make any quality seem more valuable than it really is. Sometimes intrusive condolences wore Elinor down so much that she rated good manners as more essential to comfort than a good heart.

Lady Middleton expressed her view of the affair about once a day—or twice, if it was discussed particularly often—by saying, “It really is very shocking!” This regular but gentle release allowed her to meet the Miss Dashwoods from the beginning without the slightest emotion, and very soon without remembering anything about the matter. Having thus upheld the dignity of her own sex and firmly condemned the faults of the other, she considered herself free to attend to the interests of her own parties. Since Mrs. Willoughby would be both fashionable and wealthy, she therefore decided, rather against Sir John's wishes, to leave her visiting card as soon as the marriage took place.

Colonel Brandon's sensitive, unobtrusive inquiries were never unwelcome to Elinor. His eager kindness in trying to soften her sister's disappointment had more than earned him the right to discuss it intimately, and they always spoke with trust. His chief reward for the painful effort of revealing past sorrows and present humiliations was the pity in Marianne's eyes when she sometimes looked at him, and the gentleness of her voice whenever she was obliged, or could persuade herself, to speak to him, though that did not happen often. _These_ assured him that his effort had increased her goodwill towards him. _These_ encouraged Elinor to hope that it might increase further. But Mrs. Jennings knew nothing of all this. She knew only that the Colonel remained as solemn as ever, and that she could persuade him neither to propose himself nor to authorise her to propose on his behalf. After two days she began to think the wedding would be at Michaelmas in the autumn rather than midsummer; after a week she began to think there would be no marriage at all. The understanding between the Colonel and Elinor seemed instead to suggest that the honours of the mulberry tree, the canal, and the yew arbour would fall to _her_. Mrs. Jennings had for some time stopped thinking about Mrs. Ferrars altogether.

Early in February, less than a fortnight after Willoughby's letter arrived, Elinor had the painful duty of telling Marianne that he was married. She had arranged to be informed as soon as the ceremony was known to have taken place. She did not want Marianne to learn it first from the newspapers, which she saw her eagerly searching every morning.

Marianne received the news with determined composure. She made no comment and at first shed no tears. Before long, however, they broke through, and for the rest of the day her condition was hardly less pitiable than when she had first learnt to expect the marriage.

The Willoughbys left London immediately after their wedding. With no risk now of Marianne encountering either of them, Elinor hoped to persuade her gradually to go out again as before. Since the first blow, she had never once left the house.

Around this time the two Miss Steeles, newly arrived at their cousin's house in Bartlett's Buildings, Holborn, reappeared before their grander relations in Conduit Street and Berkeley Street. Everyone welcomed them very warmly.
Only Elinor was sorry to see them. Their presence always hurt her, and she hardly knew how to respond graciously to Lucy's overwhelming delight at finding her _still_ in London.

“I should have been so disappointed if you had not been here _still_,” Lucy said repeatedly, heavily stressing the word. “But I always thought you _would_ be. I was almost sure you wouldn't leave London for a while yet, although you _told_ me at Barton, you know, that you would stay no longer than a _month_. Even then I thought you would probably change your mind when the time came. It would have been such a pity to go before your brother and his wife arrived. And now, of course, you will be in no _hurry_ to leave. I am wonderfully glad you didn't keep _your word_.”
Elinor understood her perfectly, and had to use every scrap of self-control to appear as though she did _not_.
“Well, my dear,” Mrs. Jennings asked, “how did you make the journey?”

“Not by the stagecoach, I assure you,” Miss Steele replied with immediate triumph. “We came in a hired chaise all the way, with a very smart gentleman to look after us. Dr. Davies was coming to London, so we decided to join him in a post-chaise. He behaved very handsomely and paid ten or twelve shillings more than we did.”
“Oh, oh!” Mrs. Jennings exclaimed. “Very nice indeed! And I am sure the Doctor is an unmarried man.”

“There now,” Miss Steele said, simpering affectedly, “everyone teases me so about the Doctor, and I cannot imagine why. My cousins say they are certain I have made a conquest. But I declare I never give him a thought from one hour to the next. ‘Lord, here comes your admirer, Nancy,’ my cousin said the other day, when she saw him crossing the street towards the house. My admirer, indeed! I said. I can't imagine who you mean. The Doctor is no admirer of mine.”
“Yes, yes, that sounds very pretty, but it won't do. I can see the Doctor is the one.”
“No, really!” her cousin answered with pretended earnestness. “And I beg you to contradict the story if you ever hear anyone repeat it.”
Mrs. Jennings immediately gave her the gratifying assurance that she certainly would _not_. Miss Steele's happiness was complete.
“I suppose you will stay with your brother and his wife when they come to London, Miss Dashwood,” Lucy said, returning to the attack after a pause in her hostile hints.
“No, I don't think we will.”
“Oh, I expect you certainly will.”
Elinor refused to gratify her with any further denial.
“How delightful that Mrs. Dashwood can spare both of you for such a long time at once!”
“A long time, indeed!” Mrs. Jennings interrupted. “Why, they have only just begun their visit!”
Lucy said nothing.
“I am sorry we cannot see your sister, Miss Dashwood,” said Miss Steele. “I am sorry she is unwell.” Marianne had left the room when they arrived.

“That is very kind. My sister will be equally sorry to miss the pleasure of seeing you. But lately she has suffered a great deal from nervous headaches, which make her unable to bear either company or conversation.”
“Oh dear, what a pity! But old friends like Lucy and me! Surely she could see _us_. I am certain we wouldn't say a word.”
With great politeness, Elinor declined the suggestion. Her sister might be lying on her bed, or wearing her dressing gown, and therefore unable to join them.
“Oh, if that's all,” Miss Steele exclaimed, “we can just as easily go and see _her_.”

Elinor began to feel that this intrusion was more than her temper could bear. Lucy spared her the need to stop it with a sharp rebuke of her own. Now, as often before, this did little to make one sister's manners sweeter, but usefully kept the other's under control.
